# Provenance sidecar schema

Every successful write through `dw_save()` deposits a companion file next to the primary artifact: `<path>.provenance.json`. Write `ed/dw_ed_edu.csv` and you also get `ed/dw_ed_edu.csv.provenance.json` in the same directory. The sidecar is the toolkit's record of who made the file and a way to check whether the bytes on disk have since been altered — it answers *who wrote this, when, in which session mode, from what shape of data, and does the content still match what was recorded*. Reviewer-mode integrity checks (re-hashing a file to confirm it has not changed since it was written) depend on it, which is why a producer-mode write in R or Python copies the sidecar alongside the primary file to the two backup locations the toolkit mirrors canonical files to (a Teams folder and the shared `Z:` drive); Stata's `dw_save` does not mirror. The IO contract chapter and [Vendoring and updates](../chapters/vendoring-and-updates.qmd) both lean on these checks.

The three languages diverge in one field that matters; this appendix is explicit about where.

## Where the sidecar comes from

An internal helper writes the sidecar at the end of every primary write, unless you turn it off:

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### R {.unnumbered .unlisted}
```r
# r/R/dw_io.R — .write_provenance(path, x, fmt, vintage, metadata, isid)
dw_save(df, name = "dw_ed_edu.csv", sector = "ed", kind = "wrk",
        provenance = TRUE)   # TRUE is the default; pass FALSE to skip
```
#### Python {.unnumbered .unlisted}
```python
# python/src/dw_io.py — _write_provenance(path, x, fmt, vintage, metadata, isid)
dw_save(df, name="dw_ed_edu.csv", sector="ed", kind="wrk",
        provenance=True)     # True is the default; pass False to skip
```
#### Stata {.unnumbered .unlisted}
```stata
* stata/src/dw_save.ado — sidecar emitted unless `nosidecar` is passed
dw_save, filename("dw_ed_edu.dta") path("$teamsWrkData/ed") ///
         idvars(REF_AREA INDICATOR TIME_PERIOD)
* pass the `nosidecar` option to suppress
```
:::

The R and Python helpers skip the sidecar for `.RData` / `.rda` writes, because those formats can hold arbitrary objects rather than a single tabular schema. A failed sidecar write never aborts the primary write: if a metadata value cannot be serialised to JSON, the helper warns you and leaves the primary file intact. The sidecar is metadata about the asset; the asset is what matters.

## The core schema

The following fields appear in every sidecar. The table gives the JSON key, its type, the field's meaning, and which languages emit it.

| Key | Type | Meaning | Languages |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | string | Absolute path of the primary file the sidecar describes. | R / Py / Stata |
| `format` | string | In R/Python, the dispatch format of the primary file (`"csv"`, `"parquet"`, `"dta"`, …). In Stata, a literal schema-version tag `"dw_save.provenance/1"`. | R / Py / Stata (different meaning — see below) |
| `written_at` | string | Write timestamp: ISO-8601 UTC, `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS+0000`. Stata writes it through Stata's Python integration (Stata 16+); without it, its local `c(current_date) c(current_time)`, e.g. `28 Jun 2026 14:03:51`, which the concurrent-write guard cannot compare. | R / Py / Stata |
| `user` | string | The writing user: `USERNAME`, then `LOGNAME`, `USER`, `LNAME`, then the operating system's user, in all three languages (Python: `USERNAME`, then `getpass.getuser()`, the same order). | R / Py / Stata |
| `dw_mode` | string | The session mode at write time (`"producer"`, `"reviewer"`, or unset). A session property, never a per-call argument — see the roles and mode-contract chapter. | R / Py / Stata |
| `sha256` | string \| null | Hex SHA-256 of the primary file's bytes, computed after the file is written. In R it is `null` when the optional `digest` package is not installed; Stata writes it through Stata's Python integration (Stata 16+) and omits the key without it (#191). | R / Py / Stata |
| `datasignature` | string | Stata's native `datasignature` content hash (a checksum of variable names and values), written alongside `sha256`. **Stata only.** | Stata |
| `vintage` | string \| null | Optional vintage tag (e.g. `"2026-05"`), echoed from the `vintage` argument; `null` when not supplied (Python); R writes `{}`. **R/Python only** (Stata records vintage inside `metadata`, see below). | R / Py |
| `isid` | array\<string\> \| null | The key columns asserted unique before the write (the `isid` quality contract). `null` (Python) / `{}` (R) when no uniqueness check was requested. **R/Python key is `isid`.** | R / Py |
| `idvars` | string | Stata's equivalent of `isid` — the space-separated `idvars()` columns passed to the uniqueness check. **Stata key is `idvars`.** | Stata |
| `schema` | object | The shape of the written data: `rows`, `cols`, and (R/Python only) `columns`. Empty object `{}` (Python) or empty array `[]` (R) when the object was not a data frame. | R / Py / Stata |
| `metadata` | object | The caller-supplied descriptive metadata. Present only when the caller passed `metadata` (R/Python); Stata always writes the block. | R / Py / Stata |

::: {.callout-note}
## When the session mode is unset
`dw_mode` reflects whatever the profile placed in the session state. If no profile set a mode, the key is still emitted as `null`, in R and Python alike. The key is therefore always present — a sidecar with a `null` `dw_mode` was written by a session that never declared producer or reviewer mode. (The remote-URL freeze sidecar below substitutes the literal `"unknown"` in this case; the write sidecar does not.)
:::

### The `schema` object

`schema` captures the dimensions of what was written so a reader can sanity-check a file before trusting it.

| Key | Type | Meaning | Languages |
|---|---|---|---|
| `schema.rows` | integer | Row count of the written data frame. | R / Py / Stata |
| `schema.cols` | integer | Column (variable) count. | R / Py / Stata |
| `schema.columns` | array\<string\> | Ordered list of column names. **R/Python only** — Stata records counts but not the name list. | R / Py |

### The `metadata` object

`metadata` is free-form descriptive lineage supplied by the caller. R and Python merge an arbitrary named list / mapping verbatim into the sidecar, so any key is permitted. Stata has no native nested-dictionary type. It therefore exposes a fixed set of named options plus a semicolon-separated pass-through, and closes the block with a sentinel `"_end": "true"` trailer — an artifact of writing JSON by hand, one line at a time, to avoid a dangling comma. The conventional keys, shared across languages, are:

| Key | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | string | Human-readable title of the dataset. |
| `abstract` | string | Longer description (R/Python free-form). |
| `producer` | string | The script that produced the file (e.g. `01_dw_prep/.../02_aggregate_uis_sdg.R`). |
| `sources` | array\<string\> (R/Py) / string (Stata) | Upstream data sources (e.g. `"UIS bulk SDG_092025"`, `"WPP 2024"`). |
| `contact` | string | Owner handle (e.g. `@karavan88`). |
| `vintage` | string | Data vintage; in Stata this lives inside `metadata`, in R/Python it is a top-level field as well. |
| `inputs` | array\<object\> (R, Python) | The exact input files the output was built from, one record per input: `file` (path relative to the inputs folder), `sha256`, and optionally `origin`. Pass the manifest returned by `dw_fetch_inputs()` (`manifest[, c("file", "sha256", "origin")]`). In Python pass `manifest[["file", "sha256", "origin"]]`; `dw_save` writes a DataFrame in `metadata` as an array of records, as R does. `dw_provenance_diff()` reads this record to tell whether two runs used the same inputs. |

The `inputs` record serialises as an array of objects:

```json
"metadata": {
  "title": "Global Child Targets 2030 - consolidated dataset",
  "producer": "02_consultations/023_targets/consolidate_targets.R",
  "inputs": [
    { "file": "2024/NUTRITION_2024.csv", "sha256": "5e1f…", "origin": "local" },
    { "file": "2025/WASH_2025.csv",      "sha256": "a07c…", "origin": "copied from Teams" }
  ]
}
```

## A real example (R / Python)

A write such as:

```r
dw_save(edu_sdg_uis,
        name = "dw_ed_edu.csv", sector = "ed", kind = "wrk",
        isid = c("DATAFLOW", "REF_AREA", "INDICATOR", "TIME_PERIOD"),
        vintage = "2026-05",
        metadata = list(
          title    = "Education indicators — UNICEF DW format",
          producer = "01_dw_prep/012_codes/ed/02_aggregate_uis_sdg.R",
          sources  = c("UIS bulk SDG_092025", "WPP 2024"),
          contact  = "@karavan88"
        ))
```

produces a sidecar of this shape:

```json
{
  "path": "C:/Users/.../teamsWrkData/ed/dw_ed_edu.csv",
  "format": "csv",
  "written_at": "2026-06-28T14:03:51+0000",
  "user": "jpazevedo",
  "dw_mode": "producer",
  "vintage": "2026-05",
  "sha256": "9f2c1a7b4e0d8c5f3a6b2e1d9c0f4a7b8e3d2c1f0a9b8c7d6e5f4a3b2c1d0e9f",
  "isid": ["DATAFLOW", "REF_AREA", "INDICATOR", "TIME_PERIOD"],
  "schema": {
    "rows": 48213,
    "cols": 9,
    "columns": ["DATAFLOW", "REF_AREA", "INDICATOR", "SEX",
                "WEALTH_QUINTILE", "RESIDENCE", "TIME_PERIOD",
                "OBS_VALUE", "DATA_SOURCE"]
  },
  "metadata": {
    "title": "Education indicators — UNICEF DW format",
    "producer": "01_dw_prep/012_codes/ed/02_aggregate_uis_sdg.R",
    "sources": ["UIS bulk SDG_092025", "WPP 2024"],
    "contact": "@karavan88"
  }
}
```

The Python sidecar is the same shape: the helper builds the identical key set, serialises with `json.dump(..., indent=2)`, and computes `sha256` by streaming the file in 64-KiB blocks. R serialises with `jsonlite::write_json(..., auto_unbox = TRUE, pretty = TRUE)`. The two pretty-printers differ in whitespace, and `auto_unbox` means a single-key `isid` in R collapses to a bare string rather than a one-element array — but the keys, types, and values otherwise match.

## Multi-producer lineage fields

In a project whose `cso_project.yml` sets `collaboration: multi-producer` (see the roles and mode-contract chapter), every R, Python, or Stata write adds lineage fields (R/Python after `schema` and before `metadata`; Stata after `sha256`). Single-producer sidecars, including every sidecar written in a repository without `cso_project.yml`, keep exactly the key set in the core schema above.

| Key | Type | Meaning | Languages |
|---|---|---|---|
| `collaboration` | string | Always `"multi-producer"`; marks a sidecar written under the multi-producer rules. | R / Py / Stata |
| `previous_sha256` | string \| null | SHA-256 of the file this write replaced, computed from its bytes just before the write (so after a `takeover` over an out-of-band change it is the hash of the bytes actually replaced). `null` when the output is new. | R / Py / Stata |
| `previous_user` | string \| null | `user` of the replaced file's sidecar; `null` when there was none. | R / Py / Stata |
| `previous_written_at` | string \| null | `written_at` of the replaced file's sidecar; `null` when there was none. | R / Py / Stata |
| `git_branch` | string \| null | `git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD` in the output's folder, best effort; `null` outside a repository or without git. | R / Py / Stata |
| `git_commit` | string \| null | `git rev-parse HEAD`, likewise. | R / Py / Stata |
| `takeover` | object | Present only when the write passed `takeover = TRUE`: `user`, `at` (ISO-8601 UTC) and `overrode`, the guards it overrode (`"out_of_band"`, `"concurrent"`, or an empty array when none fired). | R / Py / Stata |

`previous_sha256` chains the sidecars: each one names the bytes its write replaced, so the history of an output can be walked back without the earlier files. The guards in `dw_save()` read the same sidecar: a file whose bytes no longer match its sidecar's `sha256` was changed outside `dw_save()`, and a sidecar whose `written_at` is later than the session start and whose `user` is someone else records a concurrent write.

An API-cache write made with `refresh = TRUE` over a cache fetched by another user also records `metadata.previous_fetch` (`sha256`, `user`, `fetched_at` of the replaced fetch).

### The `baseline` object

`dw_set_collaboration()` adds one object to every sidecar that existed when the project switched, as its last key:

```json
"baseline": {
  "collaboration": "multi-producer",
  "at": "2026-11-20T10:02:17+0000",
  "by": "jpazevedo"
}
```

| Key | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `baseline.collaboration` | string | The model the project switched to. |
| `baseline.at` | string | When the switch ran (ISO-8601 UTC). |
| `baseline.by` | string | Who ran it. |

The object is inserted as text, before the sidecar's closing brace, so `sha256` and every other field keep their bytes and the out-of-band check still holds. It marks the artefact as project-owned: the first multi-producer write over it does not report a change of producer, and that write's `previous_sha256` is the baselined hash, so the lineage chain starts from the last single-producer state. Sidecars that already carry a `baseline`, or that were written under the multi-producer rules (they have `collaboration`), are left alone, which is what makes the call idempotent. A new multi-producer sidecar never carries a `baseline`. Stata sidecars receive the object too, since it is added to every `*.provenance.json`. Stata writes the lineage fields too and runs the guards through its Python integration (#168); without Python a multi-producer Stata write stops unless `takeover` is passed, and its `takeover.overrode` is then `["unguarded"]`.

## The Stata sidecar: same shape, one difference that matters

Stata emits a sidecar built to interoperate with the R and Python siblings — the comment in `dw_save.ado` states the intent plainly: "Write a sibling .provenance.json sidecar with the same shape the R helpers emit, so reviewer-mode integrity checks work across both languages." Two fields nonetheless cannot be identical, for reasons rooted in the Stata environment:

```json
{
  "format": "dw_save.provenance/1",
  "path": "C:\\Users\\...\\teamsWrkData\\ed\\dw_ed_edu.dta",
  "written_at": "2026-06-28T14:03:51+0000",
  "user": "jpazevedo",
  "dw_mode": "producer",
  "datasignature": "9:9(12345):1234567890:0987654321",
  "sha256": "4b7e0c9d2a…",
  "schema": { "rows": 48213, "cols": 9 },
  "idvars": "DATAFLOW REF_AREA INDICATOR TIME_PERIOD",
  "metadata": {
    "title": "Education indicators — UNICEF DW format",
    "producer": "01_dw_prep/012_codes/ed/02_aggregate_uis_sdg.R",
    "vintage": "2026-05",
    "_end": "true"
  }
}
```

The `datasignature` value above — `"9:9(12345):..."` — is a colon-delimited string of variable count, observation count, and two checksums, opaque by design. It is written alongside `sha256`, and is the only hash when Stata runs without Python: such a session writes no `sha256` key and a local `written_at` (`28 Jun 2026 14:03:51`).

::: {.callout-warning}
## `datasignature` is not comparable to `sha256`
With Stata's Python integration (Stata 16+) a Stata sidecar records the file's `sha256` — a hash of the file's *bytes* — as R and Python do (#191), so byte-level checks such as `dw_verify_z(compare = "sha256")` and `dw_provenance_diff()` work across all three languages. `datasignature` is extra and Stata-only: a hash of the *dataset's variables and values*, computed by Stata's built-in `datasignature` command. It is not comparable to `sha256`: a `.dta` and a `.csv` of the same logical table have different bytes (so different `sha256`) but could share a `datasignature`; conversely the same `datasignature` says nothing about file-byte equality. `datasignature` is Stata-native, needs no external dependency, and survives the UNICEF-laptop AppLocker restrictions that would block a third-party hashing binary. Without Python, Stata records only `datasignature`, and that file's integrity can be checked only inside Stata, against *its own* `datasignature`.
:::

The other differences are smaller but worth cataloguing:

- **`written_at` format.** R/Python emit ISO-8601 UTC (`2026-06-28T14:03:51+0000`). Stata emits the same through its Python integration; without it, its local human-readable clock (`28 Jun 2026 14:03:51`). A parser that wants a single timestamp type must normalise.
- **Key name for the uniqueness columns.** R/Python use `isid` (an array). Stata uses `idvars` (a single space-separated string).
- **`format` field meaning.** In R/Python `format` is the file's dispatch format (`"csv"`, `"parquet"`, …). In Stata `format` is a literal schema-version tag, `"dw_save.provenance/1"`. The same key carries different semantics — do not assume `format` tells you the file type across all three languages.
- **`schema.columns`.** Present in R/Python, absent in Stata (which records only `rows` and `cols`).
- **`vintage` placement.** A top-level field in R/Python; nested inside `metadata` in Stata.
- **`_end` sentinel.** Stata appends `"_end": "true"` as the final key of the `metadata` block — a harmless artifact of hand-writing JSON one line at a time to avoid a dangling comma. Consumers should ignore it.

## A note on the remote-URL freeze sidecar

`dw_save()` is not the only producer of `.provenance.json` files. `dw_use()` called with an allowlisted `http(s)` URL (the remote-URL freeze) downloads the file once and writes its own sidecar with a *different* shape — `url`, `sha256`, `bytes`, `fetched_at`, `fetched_by`, `dw_mode` (which falls back to the literal `"unknown"` when no mode is set). API caches written by `dw_api_fetch()` are not of this kind: they go through `dw_save()` and carry the standard write sidecar, with the fetch details in its `metadata` block. The remote-URL variant records the provenance of a network fetch rather than a local write. It shares the `.provenance.json` extension and the `dw_mode` / hashing conventions, but its key set is distinct; do not parse it with the same reader you use for the write sidecar. This appendix documents only the `dw_save()` write sidecar. Its `fetched_at` is UTC in both languages but spelled differently: R writes `2026-11-24T13:34:49Z`, Python `2026-11-24T13:34:49+0000`; a reader comparing the two should parse the timestamp rather than compare strings.

## Consuming the sidecar

A reviewer or a CI check typically does three things with a sidecar: read it, confirm the recorded `sha256` still matches the file on disk, and inspect `dw_mode` / `metadata` for lineage. Reading is plain JSON; in R and Python, `dw_read_provenance()` does it for you (output path or sidecar path; `NULL` / `None` when there is no sidecar):

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### R {.unnumbered .unlisted}
```r
prov <- dw_read_provenance("ed/dw_ed_edu.csv")
identical(prov$sha256, digest::digest(file = "ed/dw_ed_edu.csv",
                                      algo = "sha256"))
```
#### Python {.unnumbered .unlisted}
```python
import hashlib
from cso_toolkit import dw_read_provenance
prov = dw_read_provenance("ed/dw_ed_edu.csv")
h = hashlib.sha256(open("ed/dw_ed_edu.csv", "rb").read()).hexdigest()
prov["sha256"] == h
```
#### Stata {.unnumbered .unlisted}
```stata
* Stata has no JSON reader in the toolkit; verify via the native signature
use "ed/dw_ed_edu.dta", clear
datasignature
* compare r(datasignature) against the sidecar's "datasignature" value by eye
* or with a small text-parsing do-file
```
:::

A `FALSE` / `False` result here means the file changed since it was written — the lineage record no longer describes the bytes on disk, so the sidecar can no longer vouch for the artifact. R and Python can run this byte-integrity check directly because the sidecar records a byte hash, which a Stata sidecar also carries when Stata's Python integration is available. Inside Stata itself, verification uses `datasignature`: re-open the dataset, recompute it, and compare against the value in the sidecar. There is no toolkit-provided JSON reader on the Stata side — a real coverage gap, consistent with Stata's lack of an API wrapper and parquet support documented in the cross-language coverage matrix appendix.

### Comparing the sidecars of two runs

Two sidecars of the same output answer a fourth question: did the new run reproduce the previous one? In R and Python, `dw_provenance_diff(previous, current)` compares the `metadata.inputs` records (inputs) and the `sha256` fields (outputs) and returns `reproduced`, `inputs_changed` (with the input files added, removed, and changed), `output_changed` (same inputs, different output; warns), `first_run`, or `no_input_record`. Read the previous sidecar with `dw_read_provenance()` before the new run overwrites the output. Stata has no sibling (#152, closed: Stata routes through R or Python).

## Summary

Across R and Python the sidecar is effectively identical — same keys, same types, a byte-level `sha256`, ISO-8601 UTC timestamps, an `isid` array, and a full `schema.columns` list. Stata emits a parallel file with the same intent and most of the same keys, but adds `datasignature` (and, without Python, has it in place of `sha256`, with a local timestamp in place of the UTC one), uses `idvars` for `isid` and a version tag for `format`, and omits `schema.columns`. A cross-language consumer must therefore check whether a Stata sidecar carries `sha256`, normalise the timestamp when it does not, and never compare `datasignature` with an R or Python `sha256`.

Relevant source files (paths relative to the repository root):

- `r/R/dw_io.R` — `.write_provenance()` (R write sidecar) and `.write_remote_provenance()` (remote-URL freeze sidecar)
- `r/R/dw_io.R` — also the multi-producer guards and lineage fields (`.dw_collab_preflight()`) and `dw_collaboration()`
- `r/R/dw_project.R` — `dw_set_collaboration()` (writes `cso_project.yml`, inserts the `baseline` object)
- `python/src/dw_project.py` — the Python siblings of both
- `r/R/dw_provenance.R` — `dw_read_provenance()` and `dw_provenance_diff()` (read a sidecar; compare two runs)
- `r/R/dw_deposit.R` — `dw_fetch_inputs()` (returns the input manifest recorded as `metadata.inputs`)
- `python/src/dw_io.py` — `_write_provenance()`, `_sha256_file()`, `_utc_now_iso()` (Python write sidecar); `_write_remote_provenance()` (remote-URL freeze sidecar)
- `python/src/dw_provenance.py` and `python/src/dw_deposit.py` — the Python siblings of `dw_read_provenance()`, `dw_provenance_diff()` and `dw_fetch_inputs()`
- `stata/src/dw_save.ado` — Stata sidecar emission (`datasignature`, `idvars`, `format: dw_save.provenance/1`)
- `stata/src/dw_stata_helpers.py` — the Python helpers Stata calls for `sha256`, the UTC `written_at` and the multi-producer guards
- `docs/dw_io_reference.md` — sidecar field overview

::: {.callout-note}
## Microdata records provenance structurally, not in a sidecar
The survey-microdata archive — datalib's `Z:/datalib*` trees, a different data layer from the aggregate warehouse this sidecar serves — records provenance **structurally** rather than in a `.provenance.json` companion: the vintage is encoded in the IHSN folder name (`<CCC>_<YYYY>_<SSSS>_v<MM>_M` and its adaptation extension), and `Data/Original/` is kept untouched so the raw deposit is its own lineage record. Different mechanism, same intent as the sidecar — there is no datalib sidecar to document here. See the IHSN convention chapter.
:::
